content:
There has been recent discussion on how to measure the quality of AI generated Lean code. While some low-level aspects can certainly be measured deterministically (see here), it seems as though the deciding factor whether something is high quality is essentially the human eye.

Thus I propose a variation of the Turing Test for Lean code. Specifically one could do the following: Take a high quality human formalisation of some definition/theorem (ideally 1 file, not more than ~300 lines) and tell an AI agent to reformalise the main results (while not giving the agent the file obviously). Then, an expert human arbiter can rate the quality of both formalisations (maybe on a couple of aspects?) without being told which is which.

There are some caveats to this: For example one shouldn't take existing mathlib files directly as a source, since AI models are trained on mathlib. Maybe one would also strap both files of docstrings.

Doing this with say a dozen of files and a couple of arbiters (and maybe repeating the experiment every few months) could give us a somewhat quantifiable measure on how close autoformalisation quality is to the (in)famous "mathlib quality" and on what aspects autoformalisation is still lacking.

This test could also be used to for example compare different models, see how much Tau-ceti-like review helps and assess "AI quality reviewers" (something similar was done in this paper).

I would be very grateful for any help of any kind designing this study (I won't be able to do it alone) and eventually volunteer abiters of course.

So if this sounds interesting to you, please leave a message! :)
Rating takes a lot of time, but you can ask the human arbiters to identify the human-written formalisation among a sample of AI written formalisations.

This would be quite interesting to know.

But even if/when the LLM output is indistinguishable from Mathlib code, it is not the same thing as Mathlib code. To me the crucial difference is that actual Mathlib code has arisen as a consensus (or sometimes compromise) of competent humans (at least a consensus/compromise among the human contributors and reviewers, but potentially also of those Mathlib users who chose not to propose changing or refactoring the code during its existence in Mathlib). This property of the process that produced the code has value by itself, since I care about formal definitions and statements having their original (human-)intended mathematical meaning.

So while the experiment would be of interest, I really hope that one does not draw wrong conclusions about Mathlib from it.

Kalle Kytölä said:

This property of the process that produced the code has value by itself, since I care about formal definitions and statements having their original (human-)intended mathematical meaning.

A related point has been made in a different context by Anat Perry, who finds that exactly the same text will be rated as more empathic if it is human-generated than if it is AI-generated. Perry suggests that this may be because the bare text itself is not everything; it's also a signal of what else might be forthcoming from the same source in the future.
